In [[mathematics]], some '''[[boundary value problem]]s can be solved using the methods of [[stochastic processes|stochastic analysis]]'''. Perhaps the most celebrated example is [[Shizuo Kakutani]]'s 1944 solution of the [[Dirichlet problem]] for the [[Laplace operator]] using [[Brownian motion]].<ref>{{cite book 
| last = Øksendal
| first = Bernt K.
| authorlink = Bernt Øksendal
| title = Stochastic Differential Equations: An Introduction with Applications 
| edition = Sixth
| publisher=Springer
| location = Berlin 
| year = 2003 
| isbn = 3-540-04758-1
|page = 3
}}</ref> However, it turns out that for a large class of [[semi-elliptic operator|semi-elliptic]] second-order [[partial differential equations]] the associated Dirichlet boundary value problem can be solved using an [[Itō process]] that solves an associated [[stochastic differential equation]].

==History==
The link between semi-elliptic operators and stochastic processes, followed by their use to solve boundary value problems, is repeatedly and independently rediscovered in the early-mid-20th century.

The connection that Kakutani makes between stochastic differential equations and the Itō process is effectively the same as [[Kolmogorov equations|Kolmogorov's forward equation]], made in 1931, which is only later recognized as the [[Fokker–Planck equation]], first presented in 1914-1917. The solution of a boundary value problem by means of expectation values over stochastic processes is now more commonly known not under Kakutani's name, but as the [[Feynman–Kac formula]], developed in 1947.

These results are founded on the use of the [[Itō integral]], required to integrate a stochastic process. But this is also independently rediscovered as the [[Stratonovich integral]]; the two forms can be translated into one-another by an offset.

==Introduction: Kakutani's solution to the classical Dirichlet problem==

Let <math>D</math> be a domain (an [[open set|open]] and [[connected space|connected set]]) in <math display="inline">\mathbb{R}^{n}</math>. Let <math>\Delta</math> be the [[Laplace operator]], let <math>g</math> be a [[bounded function]] on the [[boundary (topology)|boundary]] <math>\partial D</math>, and consider the problem:

:<math>\begin{cases} - \Delta u(x) = 0, & x \in D \\ \displaystyle{\lim_{y \to x} u(y)} = g(x), & x \in \partial D \end{cases}</math>

It can be shown that if a solution <math>u</math> exists, then <math>u(x)</math> is the [[expected value]] of <math>g(x)</math> at the (random) first exit point from <math>D</math> for a canonical [[Brownian motion]] starting at <math>x</math>. See theorem 3 in Kakutani 1944, p.&nbsp;710.

==The Dirichlet–Poisson problem==

Let <math>D</math> be a domain in <math display="inline">\mathbb{R}^{n}</math> and let <math>L</math> be a semi-elliptic [[differential operator]] on <math display="inline">C^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{n};\mathbb{R})</math> of the form:

:<math>L = \sum_{i = 1}^{n} b_{i} (x) \frac{\partial}{\partial x_{i}} + \sum_{i, j = 1}^{n} a_{ij} (x) \frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial x_{i} \, \partial x_{j}}</math>

where the coefficients ''<math>b_{i}</math>'' and ''<math>a_{ij}</math>'' are [[continuous function]]s and all the [[eigenvalue]]s of the [[matrix (mathematics)|matrix]] ''<math>\alpha(x) = a_{ij}(x)</math>'' are non-negative. Let ''<math display="inline">f\in C(D;\mathbb{R})</math>'' and ''<math display="inline">g\in C(\partial D;\mathbb{R})</math>''. Consider the [[Poisson equation|Poisson problem]]:

:<math>\begin{cases} - L u(x) = f(x), & x \in D \\ \displaystyle{\lim_{y \to x} u(y)} = g(x), & x \in \partial D \end{cases} \quad \mbox{(P1)}</math>

The idea of the stochastic method for solving this problem is as follows. First, one finds an [[Itō diffusion]] <math>X</math> whose [[infinitesimal generator (stochastic processes)|infinitesimal generator]] <math>A</math> coincides with <math>L</math> on [[compact support|compactly-supported]] <math>C^{2}</math> functions <math>f:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}</math>. For example, <math>X</math> can be taken to be the solution to the stochastic differential equation:

:<math>\mathrm{d} X_{t} = b(X_{t}) \, \mathrm{d} t + \sigma (X_{t}) \, \mathrm{d} B_{t}</math>

where <math>B</math> is ''n''-dimensional Brownian motion, ''<math>b</math>'' has components ''<math>b_{i}</math>'' as above, and the [[tensor field|matrix field]] ''<math>\sigma</math>'' is chosen so that:

:<math>\frac1{2} \sigma (x) \sigma(x)^{\top} = a(x), \quad \forall x \in\mathbb{R}^{n}</math>

For a point <math>x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}</math>, let <math>\mathbb{P}^{x}</math> denote the law of <math>X</math> given initial datum <math>X_{0} = x</math>, and let <math>\mathbb{E}^{x}</math>denote expectation with respect to <math>\mathbb{P}^{x}</math>. Let ''<math>\tau_{D}</math>'' denote the [[Hitting time|first exit time]] of <math>X</math> from <math>D</math>.

In this notation, the [[Feasible region|candidate solution]] for (P1) is:

:<math>u(x) = \mathbb{E}^{x} \left[ g \big( X_{\tau_{D}} \big) \cdot \chi_{\{ \tau_{D} < + \infty \}} \right] + \mathbb{E}^{x} \left[ \int_{0}^{\tau_{D}} f(X_{t}) \, \mathrm{d} t \right]</math>

provided that <math>g</math> is a [[bounded function]] and that:

:<math>\mathbb{E}^{x} \left[ \int_{0}^{\tau_{D}} \big| f(X_{t}) \big| \, \mathrm{d} t \right] < + \infty</math>

It turns out that one further condition is required:

:<math>\mathbb{P}^{x} \big( \tau_{D} < \infty \big) = 1, \quad \forall x \in D</math>

For all <math>x</math>, the process <math>X</math> starting at <math>x</math> [[almost surely]] leaves <math>D</math> in finite time. Under this assumption, the candidate solution above reduces to:

:<math>u(x) = \mathbb{E}^{x} \left[ g \big( X_{\tau_{D}} \big) \right] + \mathbb{E}^{x} \left[ \int_{0}^{\tau_{D}} f(X_{t}) \, \mathrm{d} t \right]</math>

and solves (P1) in the sense that if <math>\mathcal{A}</math> denotes the characteristic operator for <math>X</math> (which agrees with <math>A</math> on <math>C^{2}</math> functions), then:

:<math>\begin{cases} - \mathcal{A} u(x) = f(x), & x \in D \\ \displaystyle{\lim_{t \uparrow \tau_{D}} u(X_{t})} = g \big( X_{\tau_{D}} \big), & \mathbb{P}^{x} \mbox{-a.s.,} \; \forall x \in D \end{cases} \quad \mbox{(P2)}</math>

Moreover, if <math display="inline">v \in C^{2}(D;\mathbb{R})</math> satisfies (P2) and there exists a constant <math>C</math> such that, for all <math>x\in D</math>:

:<math>| v(x) | \leq C \left( 1 + \mathbb{E}^{x} \left[ \int_{0}^{\tau_{D}} \big| f(X_{s}) \big| \, \mathrm{d} s \right] \right)</math>

then <math>v=u</math>.
